Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break this down simply. You’re not alone in feeling this way.

I’ll split it into two parts:

Types of roses you can choose from
Main choices when you order from us

1) Main types of roses (in plain language)

Think of these as “shapes” and “uses” of roses:

Shrub / bush roses
These are full, bushy plants. Great for most gardens and beginners. They give lots of blooms and are good for filling a space.

Climbing roses
These grow long canes that you tie to a fence, trellis, arch, or wall. Perfect if you want a rose-covered arch or wall, but they usually need a support and a bit more training.

Hybrid tea roses (classic long-stem roses)
These are the “florist-style” roses: one big, beautiful bloom per stem. Great if you want cut flowers in a vase.

Floribunda roses
These make clusters of blooms all together. Lots of color, often easier and very showy in the garden.

Groundcover / landscape roses
These stay low and spread out. Good for covering a slope, edge, or a larger area with color.

You can then pick color, fragrance (scent), and bloom style (big & classic vs. ruffly/old-fashioned) within those types.

2) Main choices when you order from us

Your climate (hardiness zone)
At the top of our website you can pick your zone so you only see roses that will live through your winters. This is important so you don’t fall in love with a rose that won’t survive where you live.

Sun needs
Most roses like full sun (at least 6 hours of direct sun daily).
Some are okay with partial shade (about 4 hours of sun). We show this as icons on the product pages.

Plant size
The height and width listed are the mature size (how big the plant will be when grown, in feet). That helps you know if it will fit your space.

Container type & planting
We sell own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil. That means:

No bare-root roses
You get a live plant in a pot that you plant in your garden or a larger container.

Delivery timing
When you check out, you can pick an estimated delivery date that works for you, so the rose arrives near when you’re ready to plant.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right things. Let’s keep it simple so you can start without feeling overwhelmed.

I’ll break it into two parts:

Things that are nice to have (optional)
Things that are really important (recommended/needed)

1) Optional but very helpful extras These help your rose settle in and grow its best, but you can still succeed without all of them.

Soil amendments (mixed into the planting hole or used around the plant):

Bone meal: Helps strong root development.
Cow manure: Adds long‑lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Loosens and aerates the soil, and can also be used as a top dressing (a layer on top of the soil) to help protect roots and hold moisture.
Worm castings: Gentle, nutrient‑rich material that improves soil structure and feeds the plant slowly.

All of these are “boosters,” not must-haves. Think of them as giving your rose a nicer home, not as something that will make or break your success.

2) Things a beginner really does need

A good sunny spot

Most roses need full sun, which means at least 6 hours of direct sunlight per day.
If a rose is marked for partial shade on our site, it can manage with around 4 hours, but more sun usually means more blooms.

Decent soil and a proper planting hole

Soil that drains well (water should not sit and stay soggy).
A hole about twice as wide as the pot the rose comes in, so roots can spread out.

Fertilizer (this is important)

Roses are hungry plants and really do better with regular feeding.
We offer fertilizers like OmniMeal and Founders Fish Fertilizer, but you can use any good rose fertilizer you prefer.
For the first year, it is best to use a liquid fertilizer instead of granular. Liquid is gentler and easier for a young plant to use.

Mulch

Mulch is a layer on top of the soil that helps keep roots cool and moist.
Our mint compost works very well as mulch.
If you use wood chips, keep them about 3 inches away from the base of the rose so the base stays dry and healthy.

Watering plan

Aim to water deeply 2 to 3 times per week, rather than a little bit every day.
Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, so the foliage stays drier.

Basic tools (simple is fine)

A small shovel for digging.
Pruners for trimming and later pruning (pruning is cutting back canes and stems to shape the plant and encourage new growth).
Gloves if you prefer, since roses do have thorns.

How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and good on you for wanting to start off right.

I’ll keep this really simple and focus on what to do the first time your rose (like Carefree Wonder) arrives.

When the box arrives
Take the rose out of the box the same day.
Set it outside in a bright spot that gets some sun.
Water the soil in the pot thoroughly so it is evenly moist (not soggy).
Decide where it will live
Roses must be grown outdoors only.
Pick a spot with:
At least 6 hours of direct sun a day (more sun = more blooms).
Soil that drains well so water doesn’t sit in a puddle.
When to plant
Plant within about 2 weeks of arrival.
Only plant in the ground if:
Your last spring frost has passed, or
You are at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
If it is not the right time where you live, move it from its shipping pot into a larger container (about 10 inches across) and keep it outdoors in a protected spot until planting time.
How to plant (ground or larger pot) Whether you plant in the ground or in a big container, the basics are the same:
Dig a hole or prepare a pot about twice as wide as the 1‑gallon pot it came in.
Gently slide the rose out of its pot and loosen the roots a little with your fingers.
Set it so the top of the root ball is level with the surrounding soil, not buried deeper.
Backfill around it with your soil. You can mix in things like compost, bone meal, or manure if you want, but they are optional.
Press the soil down lightly to remove air pockets.
Water deeply until the soil is wet all the way through.
Fertilizer and mulch (first-time use)
Wait a couple of weeks after planting before feeding.
In the first year, use a liquid fertilizer (gentler on young roots) instead of a strong granular one.
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch (like compost or fine bark) on top of the soil to keep roots cool and moist, but keep mulch a few inches away from the base of the rose itself.
First weeks of care
Water deeply 2–3 times a week, depending on heat and how fast the soil dries.
Aim water at the soil, not over the leaves.
Don’t worry if you don’t see flowers right away; the rose will focus on making roots first.
